questions.stem: A team lead uses a Claude Project to draft weekly client summaries. Her director replies to the latest one with a single line: "These still don't land." She wants to improve the summaries without guessing. What should she do FIRST?

options.text: Rewrite the Project instructions to make every weekly summary more formal and detailed, assuming the director wants a more polished style
Ask the director what missed the mark, gather two or three concrete examples, and compare them against the summaries' stated purpose
Regenerate the summary several times in the Project and send the director whichever version reads most confidently and professionally
Switch the Project to the most capable model available, since a stronger model should naturally write summaries that land better

questions.explanation: Feedback like "doesn't land" names a feeling, not a cause. Before changing anything, turn it into evidence: what was cut, what was missing, what the reader expected. Concrete examples, checked against clear success criteria, show which input to change. Changing the prompt or the model before that is a guess.

whyWrong.A: This assumes the cause is style. The gap might be missing content, wrong length or wrong focus, and a formal rewrite would not fix any of those.
whyWrong.C: Regenerating without new information produces another draft of the same kind. A confident tone is not evidence that the content now meets the director's need.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model is an expensive guess. If the summaries miss what the director needs, a stronger model will miss it too, just more fluently.

questions.mindset: Turn vague feedback into specific evidence before changing anything.

questions.stem: A marketing coordinator uses Claude to draft product announcement emails. After the first batch, the sales lead says the emails are too short and should list every feature, while the brand manager says they are too long and should focus on one key benefit. Both are senior, and the coordinator must ship the next batch on Friday. What is the BEST way to adjust?

options.text: Revise the instructions to split the difference, asking Claude for medium-length emails that cover roughly half of the listed features
Follow the sales lead's feedback in full, because longer emails with more features give customers more information to act on
Ask Claude to judge which stakeholder's feedback is more aligned with marketing best practice, and follow its recommendation for Friday's batch
Confirm with the email's owner who the audience and goal are, encode that in the instructions, and link the full feature list

questions.explanation: When feedback conflicts, the problem is an unclear goal, not the prompt wording. Settling the audience and purpose with whoever owns the email gives Claude one clear target. A secondary format, such as a linked feature sheet, can often meet the other need without weakening the main email.

whyWrong.A: Averaging two opposite requests usually satisfies neither reviewer and leaves the underlying disagreement about the email's purpose unresolved.
whyWrong.B: Picking whichever reviewer seems more persuasive skips the real question of who the email is for and who decides.
whyWrong.C: Claude cannot settle an internal business decision about audience and priorities. That choice belongs to the people accountable for Friday's batch and the outcome.

questions.mindset: Conflicting feedback is a goal problem: resolve the goal with its owner, then adjust the prompt.

questions.stem: An HR advisor added a new rule to her Project instructions after feedback: "Keep every answer under 120 words." Short questions now get better replies, but policy explanations that used to be complete now skip the eligibility steps that an older instruction requires. What is the MOST effective adjustment?

options.text: Remove the new word limit entirely and return to the previous instructions, since the earlier full answers drew no complaints
Add another line to the instructions telling Claude to follow every rule exactly and never leave out any required content
Reconcile the two rules — the limit applies except when required steps must be listed — then rerun past questions to confirm
Keep the new instructions and add the missing eligibility steps by hand whenever a policy answer comes back incomplete

questions.explanation: The two rules collide: a strict word cap cannot coexist with a requirement to always list every step. The fix is to make the instructions consistent and then **retest on a fixed set of past cases**, including both the short questions that improved and the policy answers that regressed, so the change is confirmed to help without breaking anything else.

whyWrong.A: Rolling back throws away a change that clearly helped short questions. The better move keeps the gain and removes the conflict.
whyWrong.B: Telling Claude to obey every rule does not resolve two instructions that cannot both be met. The contradiction is still there.
whyWrong.D: Manual patching makes the fix depend on someone remembering each time, and incomplete answers will slip through.

questions.mindset: Every new rule can collide with an old one; reconcile, then retest on old and new cases.

questions.stem: A sales operations analyst wanted better deal summaries, so he changed his prompt template, uploaded a new glossary to the Project and switched models, all on the same day. Overall results improved, but summaries now misname two product lines. What should he do NEXT to find the cause efficiently?

options.text: Undo the changes one at a time on a fixed set of past deals, checking product names after each, to isolate the cause
Keep all three changes and add a line to the prompt template listing the two correct product names, since results improved overall
Revert all three changes at once and return to the original setup, then redo the same three changes more carefully next week
Ask Claude in the chat to explain which of the three same-day changes made the product names come out wrong in the new summaries

questions.explanation: Changing several things at once makes it impossible to tell which one helped and which one hurt. Isolating each change against the same small set of test cases is the quickest reliable way to attribute the regression, for example to a glossary entry that conflicts with the real product names, while keeping the improvements.

whyWrong.B: Patching the symptom with a name list without finding the cause leaves the faulty change in place, and it may cause other errors that have not been noticed yet.
whyWrong.C: Reverting everything discards real improvements and repeats the same experiment without learning which change caused the problem.
whyWrong.D: Claude cannot reliably explain why its own past outputs changed across sessions and setups. Controlled comparison gives evidence; self-explanation gives a guess.

questions.mindset: Change one thing at a time, against the same test cases, so results tell you what worked.

questions.stem: A customer success manager updated her Project's reply template after repeated feedback that answers buried the next steps. Her manager asks how she knows the change worked. Which TWO pieces of evidence would BEST show the change improved results? Choose TWO.

options.text: The new replies are noticeably longer and more detailed than the replies produced under the old reply template
On ten past customer questions rerun with both templates, the share of replies passing her next-steps checklist rose
Claude rated each new reply 9 out of 10 when asked in chat to score its own answer quality
A senior executive sent a positive comment about one of the new replies, which was forwarded to her this week
Over the following two weeks at similar volume, fewer replies came back from reviewers for second-round edits than before

questions.explanation: Strong evidence compares results against agreed criteria. A **fixed before/after test set** scored with a checklist isolates the template's effect, and a **drop in rework rate** in real use, at comparable volume, shows it held up with actual reviewers. Together they cover controlled testing and real-world outcomes.

whyWrong.A: Length is not the goal. The feedback was about where next steps appear, and longer replies could even bury them further.
whyWrong.C: Self-scoring is not independent evidence. Claude grading its own answer quality without clear criteria or comparison says little about whether reviewers' complaints stopped.
whyWrong.D: One positive comment on one reply is an anecdote. It does not show a pattern across many replies or compare against the old template.

questions.mindset: Measure results against criteria, before and after, not impressions.

questions.stem: A support supervisor notices from customer survey comments that the Claude-drafted replies scoring highest all start by stating the resolution in the first sentence, followed by a short apology. Only some agents' drafts do this. Which TWO actions would MOST reliably make this pattern standard for the whole team? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add a rule to the team's shared Project instructions saying replies must open with the resolution, then a brief apology
Ask each agent to tell Claude in their own individual chats to remember this new pattern for future conversations
Switch the whole team to a more capable model, since the higher-scoring replies were probably produced by better reasoning
Upload two of the highest-scoring replies to the Project knowledge as approved examples of the expected opening structure
Share the survey results in the team channel and encourage the agents to regenerate drafts until each opening looks right

questions.explanation: Positive feedback tells you what to keep. Capturing it in **shared Project instructions** (the rule) and **approved examples in Project knowledge** (what it looks like) makes it apply to every chat in that Project for everyone, instead of depending on individual habits. Instructions plus examples is also more reliable than instructions alone.

whyWrong.B: Relying on each agent's individual chats is inconsistent and depends on everyone remembering. The shared Project is the durable, team-wide place.
whyWrong.C: The survey points to structure, not reasoning depth. A bigger model does not tell Claude which structure customers prefer.
whyWrong.E: Encouragement plus regeneration leaves the outcome to chance and adds effort on every reply.

questions.mindset: When feedback reveals what works, make it the default for everyone, not a habit for some.

questions.stem: A program manager asks Claude for a five-section project kickoff brief. Sections 1, 2, 4 and 5 are exactly right, but section 3, on risks, is too technical for the steering committee. What is the BEST follow-up message?

options.text: "Not quite right. Please try the whole brief again and make it better for the steering committee this time."
"Start over with a fresh version of the brief, and this time write the entire document in simpler language."
"Keep sections 1, 2, 4 and 5. Rewrite only section 3 for executives: plain language, top three risks, with impact and owner."
"Section 3 is wrong. Are you sure this is right? Please double-check it and fix any problems you find."

questions.explanation: Specific feedback tells Claude what to keep, what to change and what the target looks like. Naming the audience and the shape of the fix gets a targeted revision without putting the four good sections at risk.

whyWrong.A: Vague feedback produces a different draft with new problems and may change the sections that were already right.
whyWrong.B: Rewriting everything risks losing four good sections to fix one, and it still does not say what the committee needs from the risks section.
whyWrong.D: Asking Claude whether it is sure does not explain what is wrong. The issue is audience fit, not a factual error to self-check.

questions.mindset: Good feedback says what to keep, what to change and what good looks like.

questions.stem: A strategy analyst has revised her prompt five times for a competitor landscape summary. Each round reads better, but the product team keeps sending the same feedback: the pricing and recent launches are months out of date. What is the MOST effective change of approach?

options.text: Add an instruction telling Claude to use only the most current pricing and launch information it already knows about
Ask Claude to add a confidence score next to each competitor fact so readers can judge which facts are reliable
Keep refining the prompt wording, since each revision has improved the summary and the remaining gap now seems small
Switch to research mode or supply current sources, so the summary draws on up-to-date information that can be checked

questions.explanation: The feedback is consistent and specific: the facts are stale. That is a missing-information problem, so further rewording cannot fix it. Switching to an approach that brings in current sources (research mode or web search, or documents she provides) addresses the cause, and grounding the summary in sources she can check makes the facts verifiable.

whyWrong.A: Instructing Claude to be current does not give it newer information, and pressing for facts it does not have invites confident fabrication.
whyWrong.B: Self-reported confidence scores are not a reliable check of whether a fact is current, and they leave the stale data in place.
whyWrong.C: Five rounds of the same feedback show the wording is not the issue. More polishing works on the wrong problem.

questions.mindset: When the same feedback survives several rewrites, change the approach, not the wording.

questions.stem: An operations team uses a faster, lower-cost model for all of its Claude work to keep costs down. Results show product tagging is fine, but drafts of sensitive escalation emails to key accounts come back from managers with heavy rewrites almost every time. What is the BEST adjustment?

options.text: Move all of the team's tasks to the most capable model, since the escalation results show the lighter model is not good enough
Use a more capable model for the escalation emails only, keep the lighter model for tagging, and compare manager rewrite rates before and after
Keep the lighter model for everything and ask managers to accept more rewrites, because the cost savings outweigh the extra editing
Stop using Claude for escalation emails and have managers write them from scratch, since the results show Claude cannot handle them

questions.explanation: The results split by task: simple, high-volume tagging meets the bar on the lighter model, while nuanced, high-stakes writing does not. Matching the model to each task, then measuring whether rewrites drop, balances quality and cost. Heavy rework can cost more than the savings.

whyWrong.A: Upgrading everything ignores evidence that tagging already works, and spends more on a task that does not need it.
whyWrong.C: Constant manager rewrites are a real cost. Saving model usage while rework stays high is not an optimization.
whyWrong.D: Dropping the use case overreacts to one setup problem. A better-matched model is worth testing first.

questions.mindset: Let results by task drive model choice: light where it meets the bar, stronger where it does not.

questions.stem: A facilities manager publishes Claude-drafted FAQ answers on the staff intranet. The help-desk log shows that almost every answer generates follow-up questions such as "What does HVAC zone mean?" and "Who do I actually contact?" Which TWO actions would BEST turn this feedback into a lasting improvement? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to make each answer more comprehensive by adding background on how the building's core systems work
Switch to a more capable model so the answers become more accurate about the building's technical systems
Update the instructions to name the audience as non-technical staff, avoid or explain jargon, and always name a contact
Ask Claude to review each draft answer and confirm it is accurate before the manager publishes it to the intranet
Track how many follow-up questions each answer receives before and after the change, to confirm the fix is working

questions.explanation: The follow-up questions are direct evidence of an **audience mismatch**: jargon and a missing contact. Fixing the instructions addresses that cause, and tracking follow-up volume before and after turns the help-desk log into a measure of whether the fix actually worked.

whyWrong.A: More background adds length and possibly more jargon. Readers asked for plain terms and a contact, not more technical depth.
whyWrong.B: Accuracy is not the complaint. The answers may be correct but unreadable for this audience; a bigger model does not change the target reader.
whyWrong.D: A self-check confirms accuracy, which was not the problem, and it does nothing about jargon or the missing contact details.

questions.mindset: Readers' follow-up questions show what the output is missing; fix the audience, then measure.

questions.stem: A communications specialist has refined a Claude-based template for internal announcements over three rounds. On her set of 12 test requests, 11 now meet every agreed criterion. The remaining comments come from one reviewer who prefers different word choices, and each extra round takes about an hour. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Adopt the template with a quick human review before sending, note the reviewer's preferences, and revisit only if new issues appear
Continue refining until the reviewer has no further comments, since any remaining feedback means the template is not finished
Rebuild the template from scratch with a different structure, since three rounds of iteration have not produced zero comments
Move the template to the most capable model and run all 12 test requests again to see whether the word choices improve

questions.explanation: Iteration should stop when results meet the agreed criteria and further rounds give diminishing returns. Eleven of twelve passing, with the rest down to personal word choice, is good enough to adopt with a light review. Recording the preferences keeps the option open without spending hours chasing taste.

whyWrong.B: Chasing one reviewer's taste ignores the agreed criteria and turns each hour of effort into very little improvement.
whyWrong.C: Starting over discards a template that already meets the bar, which is the opposite of acting on results.
whyWrong.D: Word preference is not a capability gap. A bigger model costs more and gives no particular reason to match one person's taste.

questions.mindset: Stop iterating when results meet the agreed bar; diminishing returns are a result too.

questions.stem: A compliance analyst asks Claude to summarize vendor contracts and flag risk clauses. Her review log shows the summaries are reliable for contracts under about 15 pages, but on long master agreements Claude regularly misses clauses near the end. What is the MOST effective adjustment?

options.text: Add a sentence to the prompt telling Claude to read the entire document carefully and not miss any risk clauses
Stop using Claude for long master agreements and have a senior reviewer check those contracts entirely by hand from now on
For long agreements only, have Claude review the contract section by section, then combine the flagged clauses into one summary
Ask Claude at the end of each summary to list clauses it may have missed and append them to the output

questions.explanation: The log narrows the problem to one condition: long documents. Breaking those into smaller steps (task decomposition) gives each section full attention, and limiting the change to long agreements keeps the simple process for contracts that already work.

whyWrong.A: Telling Claude to be careful does not change how the task is structured. The same failure is likely on long documents.
whyWrong.B: Dropping Claude for long contracts overreacts. A structural change is worth testing first, with human review where the stakes require it.
whyWrong.D: A model that missed a clause is not a reliable judge of what it missed. This adds a step without a real check.

questions.mindset: Segment results to find where it fails, then change the approach only where it fails.

questions.stem: Several analysts on a team share one Claude Project for client reports. Each has been telling Claude in their own chats to use the client's fiscal year rather than the calendar year, but new reports from the team still keep using calendar years. Where should this correction live so it applies MOST reliably?

options.text: In each analyst's personal preference settings, so the fiscal-year rule applies to all of that analyst's own conversations
In the shared Project's instructions, so it applies to every chat in that Project for everyone on the team
In the team's most recent chat, so analysts can scroll back and copy the correction whenever they start a report
In a note in the team's handbook reminding analysts to check fiscal years before they send in each report

questions.explanation: The correction belongs to the client work, not to any one person or chat. **Project instructions** apply across all chats inside that Project, so the rule reaches every analyst automatically, and updating it once updates it for the whole team.

whyWrong.A: Personal settings belong to one user and follow them everywhere: analysts who never set the rule are missed, and a client-specific rule leaks into unrelated work.
whyWrong.C: A correction left in one chat does not carry into new chats and depends on people remembering to find and copy it.
whyWrong.D: A handbook reminder keeps the fix manual. It catches errors after drafting instead of preventing them.

questions.mindset: Put recurring corrections at the scope where the work lives: shared Project for team work.

questions.stem: A brand team runs the same five-step brand-compliance check on every piece of copy, across several different Projects. Feedback shows people keep correcting Claude on the same steps, such as forgetting the trademark-symbol rule. Which TWO actions would BEST turn this feedback into a lasting improvement? Choose TWO.

options.text: Package the five-step check, with the trademark rule and an approved example, as a Skill the team can reuse wherever relevant
Paste the five steps into the first message of each new chat so Claude has the procedure every time work starts
Rerun a few past pieces of copy that had the errors and confirm the packaged check catches them without new mistakes
Ask Claude at the end of each check whether it remembered the trademark rule and to add it if it did not
Create a separate Project for every campaign the team runs and copy the full five-step procedure into each Project's instructions

questions.explanation: A repeatable procedure used across many Projects is what **Skills** are for: packaged instructions and resources Claude loads when relevant. Then **retest on past failures** to confirm the change fixes the reported errors without introducing new ones.

whyWrong.B: Re-pasting the steps each time is the repetition the feedback exposed. It depends on every person remembering every time.
whyWrong.D: Asking afterward whether it remembered is a self-check, not a fix. The step can still be skipped or done wrong.
whyWrong.E: Copying the procedure into many Projects multiplies maintenance, and every copy must be updated when the procedure changes.

questions.mindset: A repeated procedure across contexts belongs in a reusable package, and every fix gets retested.

questions.stem: Over six months, a recruiting coordinator has added a new line to her Project instructions after nearly every piece of feedback. The instructions are now 60 rules long, some refer to a process the team no longer uses, and recent results show drafts take more back-and-forth and occasionally follow outdated steps. What is the BEST adjustment?

options.text: Review the rules, remove outdated ones, merge overlaps, and resolve conflicts, then retest with recent requests that had problems
Add a new rule at the top telling Claude to prioritize the most recent rules over older ones when they conflict
Move all 60 rules into a document in Project knowledge so the instructions field looks shorter and easier to read
Start a fresh Project with no instructions and add rules back only when someone sends the same complaint a second time

questions.explanation: Feedback-driven rules need maintenance too. Outdated and conflicting rules are now the cause of the poor results. Pruning and consolidating removes the cause, and retesting on recent problem requests confirms the cleaned-up set works.

whyWrong.B: Claude has no reliable way to tell which rules were added most recently, and the outdated rules are still there causing confusion.
whyWrong.C: Moving the same rules into a file keeps every conflict and outdated step. It only changes where they sit.
whyWrong.D: Discarding everything throws away the rules that work and repeats months of the same feedback cycle.

questions.mindset: Instructions built from feedback need pruning; more rules is not always better results.
